cards.front: Stylised Raiffeisenbank liquid assets (market value): central-bank reserves €120m; non-covered-bond Level 1 EU sovereign bonds €80m; AA covered bonds (Level 2A) €60m; qualifying RMBS (Level 2B) €40m. Apply the LCR haircuts (L1 0%, L2A 15%, L2B RMBS 25%); no cap binds. What is the post-haircut liquidity buffer in €m?

Same balance sheet. Gross 30-day outflows total €340m. Inflows: performing retail repayments €60m at 50% and FI receivables €40m at 100%. With the standard 75% inflow cap, compute the 30-day stressed net cash outflow NCO\(_{30}\) in €m.
With a buffer of €281m and NCO\(_{30}\) of €270m, what is the LCR (as a fraction)? Does it clear the minimum?

Starting from buffer €281m and NCO €270m, supervision rejects the 'stable' tag on €600m of retail deposits, reclassifying them from the 5% to the 10% run-off rate. Assets are unchanged. What is the new LCR (as a fraction)?
Derive the LCR buffer for the stylised book: reserves €120m, non-covered L1 sovereigns €80m, L2A covered bonds €60m, L2B RMBS €40m. Apply haircuts and the adjusted-amount caps in sequence.

steps.prompt: Post-haircut non-covered Level 1 = reserves + sovereigns at 0% haircut?
Does the 40% Level-2 cap bind? Test L2 total 81 against 2/3 × adjusted L1 (= 2/3 × 200 = 133.3).
steps.explain: 81 < 133.3, so the 40% cap does not bind; the 15/85 L2B sub-cap (44.3) also does not bind.

steps.prompt: Buffer = sum of eligible amounts in €m?

cards.front: In the LCR buffer, non-covered-bond Level 1 must be at least {{c1}} of the buffer (composition floor); total Level 2 may not exceed {{c2}}; and within that, Level 2B is sub-capped at {{c3}}. These caps bite on the Annex I {{c4}} amounts, not on the raw post-haircut total.

LCR inflows are normally capped at {{c1}} of gross outflows, so HQLA must cover at least {{c2}} of the drain. Specialised/promotional lenders may use a {{c3}} cap, and fully pass-through intragroup/IPS and promotional flows can be {{c4}} from the cap.

NSFR factors: regulatory capital and >1y liabilities score {{c1}} ASF; stable retail/SME deposits <1y score {{c2}} ASF; performing residential mortgages (≤35% RW) carry {{c3}} RSF; and a flat {{c4}} RSF add-on is charged on gross derivative liabilities.

The sector Leitfaden Liquidität prescribes a single, uniform deposit-classification taxonomy (stable / less-stable / operational, plus the DGS-covered vs. excess split) used by every member Raiffeisenbank. Is this taxonomy a CRR-forced regulatory value or an ÖRS proportionality choice — and what is the produced tradeoff?
rubric: Separates the two layers: the DelVO hard-wires the run-off RATES (reg), but bucketing each deposit into stable/less-stable/operational is the bank's/sector's modelling freedom (ors).
Produces the upside of the uniform taxonomy: comparability across members, central-function efficiency, and defensibility before the Aufsichtsrat.

Produces the cost: a standard taxonomy can be more conservative than a tailored local model for an atypical member, sacrificing buffer headroom — proportionality means small members accept the standard rather than build bespoke behavioural models.

cards.front: A risk officer claims 'the whole LCR denominator is a bank modelling choice.' True or false? Separate what the DelVO fixes from the bank's freedom, and state the tradeoff.
rubric: Reg-fixed: every run-off and inflow rate (stable retail 5%, non-operational NFC 40%, unsecured FI 100%, inflow cap 75%) is hard-wired by the DelVO for cross-bank comparability.
Bank freedom: ONLY the classification — is the deposit stable? is the portion operational? is the collateral Level 1? — which is where supervisory scrutiny concentrates.
Tradeoff: fixed rates buy comparability at the cost of risk-sensitivity; since classification is the only lever, a defensible deposit-stability narrative (ILAAP) is examined as hard as the number.

cards.front: Defend to the Aufsichtsrat why the framework needs BOTH the LCR and the NSFR — why is one not redundant given the other?

rubric.text: States the LCR is a 30-day stock/cash test while the NSFR is a one-year structural funding test (ASF ÷ RSF).

Gives the canonical failure the other misses: a government-bond buffer funded entirely with 1-month wholesale passes the LCR but fails the NSFR because short funding (0% ASF) of a non-trivially-liquid asset is penalised.
Concludes neither subsumes the other — tactical 30-day survival vs. strategic term-funding structure.

antiPoints: Claiming the NSFR is just the LCR over a longer horizon with the same mechanics.
Saying one ratio replaces the other for small banks under proportionality.
Confusing the 75% inflow cap (an LCR mechanic) with an NSFR feature.
cards.modelAnswer: The LCR is a tactical stock test: enough HQLA, after haircuts and caps, to cover the net cash that drains out over an acute 30-day stress. The NSFR is a structural one-year test that weights funding by stability (ASF) and assets by required stable funding (RSF). They are not redundant because a bank can hold a vast govvie buffer that sails through the LCR yet fund it with one-month wholesale paper — fine on day 1, but on day 31 the paper matures into a shut market, which only the NSFR (0% ASF against a positive-RSF asset) catches. One is the 30-day siege test, the other the term-funding test; neither subsumes the other.

cards.front: Place the ILAAP against the ICAAP for the board: how do they relate, and why must their stress scenarios be consistent?

rubric.text: Identifies the ILAAP as the liquidity counterpart of the ICAAP — both board-owned internal adequacy processes that feed the SREP (where a weak ILAAP can trigger Pillar 2 liquidity guidance/add-ons).
Distinguishes the resources: ICAAP = capital / loss absorption; ILAAP = liquidity & funding / payment capacity, with metrics like survival period, counterbalancing capacity and internal stress LCR.

Explains consistency: a liquidity stress that forces asset fire-sales crystallises losses and consumes capital, so the two sets of adverse scenarios must be mutually consistent — two readings of one stressed balance sheet.

antiPoints: Saying the ILAAP replaces the ICAAP for liquidity-rich banks.
Calling the ILAAP a pure payment-systems report.
Claiming the two processes are unrelated.
cards.modelAnswer: The ILAAP is to liquidity what the ICAAP is to capital: both are internal, board-owned adequacy processes that feed the SREP, and both run the same normative-plus-economic two-perspective logic. The ICAAP asks whether the bank can absorb losses over the horizon; the ILAAP asks whether it can meet outflows and stay funded, using metrics like the survival period, counterbalancing capacity and an internal stress LCR. Their scenarios must be consistent because a liquidity stress that forces fire-sales realises losses and so consumes capital — they are two readings of a single stressed balance sheet, and a weak ILAAP can attract Pillar 2 liquidity add-ons.

cards.front: A junior analyst computes the Level 2B sub-cap as 15% of the raw post-haircut HQLA total. Defend why this is wrong and state the correct mechanism.

rubric.text: States the 40% and 15% caps bite on the Annex I ADJUSTED amounts produced by the unwinding algorithm (unwind every short-term secured transaction collateralised with HQLA back to cash), not on the raw post-haircut total.

Gives the operational form: total Level 2 ≤ 2/3 of adjusted Level 1 (→ 40% of the whole), and L2B ≤ 15/85 of (Level 1 + capped L2A) (→ 15%); when a cap binds the excess is EXCLUDED from the buffer entirely, not down-weighted.
Notes the shortcut coincides only when no cap binds and no secured-transaction unwinding shifts the composition; a repo against your sovereigns or a covered-bond-heavy buffer breaks it.

antiPoints: Asserting the flat 15%-of-raw-total shortcut is always correct.
Saying excess Level 2B is merely down-weighted rather than excluded.
Claiming Level 1 is uniformly uncapped and zero-haircut (ignoring the 7% EHQ covered-bond haircut and the 30% floor).
cards.modelAnswer: The shortcut is wrong because the DelVO Annex I caps act on adjusted amounts, not the raw post-haircut total: the algorithm first unwinds every short-term secured-funding/lending/collateral-swap transaction collateralised with HQLA back to cash, then applies the limits to that unwound composition. Operationally this reduces to total Level 2 ≤ 2/3 of adjusted Level 1 (the 40% cap) and L2B ≤ 15/85 of Level 1 plus capped L2A (the 15% sub-cap), and any excess is excluded from the buffer outright rather than down-weighted. The flat-15%-of-total trick only happens to match when no cap binds and no repo against HQLA shifts the composition; the moment a sovereign repo or a covered-bond-heavy buffer moves the mix, it over- or under-states the eligible buffer, so you must run the algorithm.
